name: Azure DevOps
card_surface: Azure DevOps board cards expose VCS state through 'Annotations', a per-team setting toggled in board configuration (Boards > Settings > Annotations). Native annotations include Tasks (child item count with check progress), Tests (requirement-based test suite count and pass/fail dot), and GitHub annotations (commits, PRs, issues) when GitHub is linked. Each annotation appears as a small icon plus a numeric count at the bottom of the card; a coloured dot encodes status (green = succeeded/closed, red = failed, grey = pending). For first-party Azure Repos, there is no dedicated PR-count or branch-name annotation on the card face by default; PR/branch state lives in the Development control inside the work item form. The card body itself surfaces only configured fields (Title, Assigned To with avatar, State pill, Tags, Effort/Story Points, parent name, and any custom fields the team adds). The card stays compact: most VCS detail (branch name, PR title, PR number, CI status) is intentionally deferred to the detail form, so the card face stays around two to three rows of metadata plus optional annotation icons. With the May 2025 Azure Boards + GitHub Copilot integration, an additional inline indicator appears on the card when Copilot is working on the item or has a draft PR ready for review.
detail_panel: The expanded work item form has a dedicated 'Development' control that lists every linked Branch, Commit, Pull Request, and Build in a single block. Each PR row shows: PR title (clickable), PR number (#id), state (Active, Draft, Completed, Abandoned) rendered with a coloured icon, target branch, and a link out to the PR page. Branch rows show repo name + branch name; commit rows show the abbreviated SHA, message, author and timestamp. A 'Maximize Development' affordance expands the control to show all link types side by side. A separate 'Deployment' control surfaces release pipeline stage status (e.g. Dev succeeded, Staging in progress, Prod pending) for two stages at a time, with a status dot per stage and a link to the release run. Build links surface under 'Found in build' and 'Integrated in build'. The Links tab lists every artifact link including Branch, Build, Changeset, Commit, Found in build, Integrated in build, Pull Request, and Versioned Item, and a Related Work tab lists parent/child work items. Reviewer state, CI check breakdown and inline diff do not live on the work item form itself - the PR detail page is the canonical surface for that information, reached via the PR link inside the Development control.
state_coupling: Azure DevOps couples PR state to work item state more tightly than most peers. When a PR is created from the work item (or linked manually) and 'Complete linked work items after merging' is selected on the PR, completing/merging the PR automatically transitions every linked work item into its terminal completed-state-category state (Closed for Agile/CMMI, Done for Scrum/Basic). The setting is opt-in per PR but the user's last choice is remembered as the default for future PRs in that repo. Authors can also override the transition target per work item by adding a prefix in the PR description (e.g. 'Fixes #1234' or '#1234 resolved') - Azure DevOps recognises common keywords and applies the matching workflow transition. A repository-level 'Automatically complete work items' switch enables the behaviour globally. The system will refuse to auto-advance the work item when (a) the work item is already in the completed-state-category, (b) a workflow rule blocks the transition (e.g. a required field is empty), or (c) the rule prevents skipping intermediate states. Branch creation, commit, PR open and CI pass do NOT trigger automatic state changes by themselves - only PR completion does. Granularity is per PR (UI checkbox) and per repository (automatic completion toggle); there is no per-board or per-column rule. Teams that want finer automation (e.g. move to In Review when a PR opens) typically use Power Automate, Azure Logic Apps, or extensions such as 'Workflow' or 'Automate Azure DevOps'.
draft_vs_ready_state: Draft PRs are a first-class state since Sprint 143 (late 2018). A draft PR is created via 'Create as draft' in the PR creation dialog or the '--draft true' flag in the az CLI, and an active PR can be demoted via 'Mark as draft' from the PR overview menu (which clears all existing votes). In the work item form's Development control, draft PRs render with a distinct draft icon (grey/outlined pull request glyph) and the PR title is prefixed with a 'Draft' label so a reviewer can tell at a glance the PR is not yet up for review. Required reviewers are not notified for drafts, build policies still run but are not blocking, and auto-complete cannot be set while a PR is draft. Draft PRs can still carry work item links, reviewers, comments and commits, but completing the PR is disabled until 'Publish' is clicked. The card face itself does not differentiate draft vs. ready unless a team adds a custom annotation extension or surfaces the linked-PR state as a card field; out of the box the distinction is only visible inside the form.
review_state: Reviewer status is surfaced on the PR page, not directly on the board card. Each reviewer appears as an avatar with a coloured vote glyph: green tick (Approved), green tick with star (Approved with suggestions), grey clock (Waiting for author), red X (Rejected), and a person icon for 'No vote'. Reviewers are flagged as Required (must approve to merge, set by branch policy or PR author) or Optional (vote counted but not blocking). The PR overview shows a summary line such as '2 of 3 required reviewers approved' alongside the branch policy panel that lists every required check (Build validation, Required reviewers, Status checks, Linked work items). On the work item Development control the PR row shows only state (Active, Draft, Completed, Abandoned) and number of required approvals satisfied; individual reviewer avatars do not surface there. The board card does not show reviewer state unless a marketplace extension (e.g. 'Pull Request Manager Hub', 'Card Annotations') is installed; the canonical place to triage reviews is the My Pull Requests page or the per-PR view.
dod_checklist: There is no first-class Definition of Done field on the work item type. The native pattern is to use child Tasks (a separate work item type) under a User Story / Product Backlog Item; the Tasks render as a Checklist annotation on the parent card (count + completion progress, e.g. '3 of 5'). The Acceptance Criteria field is a free-text rich-text field on User Story / PBI / Requirement and is the closest native DoD surface, but it is plain markdown and is not gated. To get checkbox-style DoD with templates, teams install marketplace extensions such as 'Definition of Done' (agile-extensions.dod) which adds a DoD tab inside the work item form with per-work-item-type templates, persistent state, and completion percentage, or 'Appgami Checklist' which adds reusable checklist templates that auto-populate on new work items. None of these are first-party. DoD does NOT gate state transitions in either the native task-checklist pattern or the extensions - teams sometimes wire a branch policy or work item rule to require checklist completion, but it is custom. Completion percentage is computed from child tasks when rollup columns are enabled; the card face shows only the count and a completion bar, the form shows the list.
test_linkage: Test management is first-party and deeply integrated. Test Plan, Test Suite, and Test Case are all native work item types under Azure Test Plans. Test Cases link to requirements (User Story / PBI / Requirement / Issue / Bug) via the typed 'Tested By / Tests' link. When the user clicks the inline 'Add test' affordance on a board card, Azure DevOps creates a Test Case and automatically attaches it via the requirement-based suite, which causes a Tests annotation to appear on the card (test count + pass/fail dots derived from the latest test run results in the linked Test Plan). Cards display: number of associated tests, a coloured status dot per test (green pass, red fail, grey not run, blue blocked), and the option to run tests directly from the card. The work item form has a Test tab listing every linked test case with status, outcome and the latest test run. Automated tests can be associated to a Test Case via the 'Associate automated test' workflow inside Visual Studio or via the REST API, after which the next pipeline run reports outcomes back to the Test Case. CI pass/fail (the pipeline result) is a separate concern from the Test Case status: the pipeline link appears under 'Integrated in build' in the Development control, and the test results from that build attach to their respective Test Cases. SharedSteps and SharedParameter link types support re-use across cases. Third-party test tools (TestRail, Tricentis, Xray for Azure DevOps) exist but are rarely needed because the native experience is already first-class.
cicd_status: Pipeline status is surfaced in three places. (1) The work item Development control lists 'Integrated in build' links - each shows the pipeline name, build number, and a status icon (green check succeeded, red X failed, blue spinning building, grey pending). Clicking through goes to the pipeline run summary. (2) The Deployment control shows release-pipeline stage status per environment with the same icon vocabulary - this gives the work item form a per-stage CI/CD strip. Classic release pipelines populate this automatically when 'Report deployment status to Boards' is enabled; YAML pipelines now populate it as well (rolled out 2024). (3) On the PR page, every status check posted via the Status API renders as a row with a state icon (succeeded / failed / pending / error) plus description and a link to the build. Build validation policies block PR completion until the build succeeds; status policies (from external services) work the same way. The board card itself does NOT show CI status as a standalone annotation - only the Build annotation count via GitHub annotation when GitHub is the source, or via the Tasks/Tests annotations indirectly. Failing CI is therefore visible on the PR and the work item form but is not surfaced as a card-level red signal unless a team adds a custom field that mirrors latest build status. Azure Pipelines is the native CI provider; external CI providers (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, CircleCI) integrate via the Status API and appear in the same surfaces.
release_tagging: The release container is split across three concepts. (1) Iteration Path is the canonical sprint/PI assignment field on every work item, hierarchical (e.g. Project\Release 1\Sprint 3). (2) The 'Tags' field is a free-text multi-value tag list and is commonly used as a soft 'fix-version' label (e.g. 'release-2025.04'); tags can be coloured per board. (3) Git tags / Releases in Azure Repos are independent of work items but become linked via the Deployment control once a release pipeline runs against a tagged commit. There is no native 'Fix Version' object equivalent to Jira's Fix Version. Marketplace extensions ('Release Plans for Azure DevOps', 'Delivery Plans') add release-like container objects. A story can implicitly belong to multiple releases because Tags is multi-value and because a commit linked to the work item can be tagged in several Git tags. The card face shows Iteration Path (often abbreviated as the sprint name) and Tags only if the team configured them under Board > Fields; release-tag style data does not appear by default. Release scope changes are tracked via the work item history (Iteration Path or Tag changes) rather than as a structured event log.
aggregation: Aggregation works for counts, story points and progress, but NOT for VCS state. Native rollup columns added to a backlog or query view sum child story points, total work, and completion percentage onto parent Features and Epics (e.g. 'Progress by Work Items' renders a bar showing % of descendants closed, and 'Progress by Story Points' renders a bar weighted by points). Rollup columns can be added under Column Options > Add rollup column. However, neither the card face nor the form aggregates PR count, branch count, CI status or test pass-rate from child Stories to the parent Feature/Epic. A Feature card cannot natively show '3 of 5 stories have merged PRs' or 'CI failing on 2 of 5 children'. The only indirect VCS signal that rolls up is via state: when child stories are auto-completed by PR merge and the team has the 'Update Parent' workflow rule enabled (or installs the 'AzDo Open in Excel'/Workflow extensions), the Feature progress bar moves. Identifying this gap is widely-cited feedback in Developer Community threads. Marketplace extensions ('Roll-up Board', 'Power BI Analytics views') reconstruct a richer rollup but remain bolt-on.
environment_deployment_target: Environment deployment is a first-class native surface via the Deployment control on the work item form. Each linked release pipeline stage renders as a row with the environment name (Dev / QA / Staging / Prod, defined in the pipeline), a status icon (succeeded, in progress, failed, queued, canceled), a timestamp, and a deep link to the release run / stage. The control shows two stages at a time with a 'View all stages' overflow. Classic release pipelines wire this up automatically by enabling 'Report deployment status to Work' under Pipeline Options > Integrations. YAML pipelines wire it up via the Environments resource and (since 2024) report stage status into the same Deployment control - including for GitHub-hosted repos. Multiple environments are shown simultaneously per work item, so a story can read as 'Dev: succeeded, Staging: succeeded, Prod: pending approval'. The board card face does NOT surface deployment-environment badges by default; the signal lives in the form. For RTE / PM personas this means deployment status is only one click away (open card > Deployment control) but is not a column-board summary unless a custom field mirrors the latest stage. The 'Integrated in release' link type ties the data model together.
traceability_completeness: There is no native composite traceability indicator. Azure DevOps exposes the underlying data (linked branch + linked PR + linked build + linked release stage + linked test case + child tasks complete) on the work item form, and one can write a custom query to find work items missing any of those links, but the platform does not render a single composite badge such as 'Code + Tests + Deploy + DoD all complete' on the card. Closest native approximations: (1) the 'Progress by Work Items' rollup column already gives a single % bar for child completion; (2) the Definition of Done extension shows a DoD completion percentage in the form. Traceability completeness does not gate state transitions natively - work items can be Closed with no linked PR, no linked test, and an empty Acceptance Criteria, unless a team configures custom work item rules (e.g. 'Closed requires Linked Pull Request' via inherited process or the marketplace extension 'TFS Aggregator'). Reporting tools (Power BI Analytics, the Traceability sample report) can surface a cross-section of which work items have full traceability, but it is a report, not a card affordance. For an EAP prototype the Azure DevOps lesson is that the raw data exists and is uniquely well-linked (especially via Development + Deployment controls), but the composite UI signal is the gap any tool can still differentiate on.
design_pattern: The dominant pattern is multi-control panel: VCS state is segmented into named, expandable controls on the work item form - Development (branches, commits, PRs, builds), Deployment (release stages), Test (linked test cases with run results), and Related Work (parent/child/related). Each control uses a uniform vocabulary of small status icons (green check, red X, grey clock, blue spinner) plus a textual label, no coloured pill fills, no count badges. On the card face the pattern is icon + numeric count via Annotations, opt-in per team and limited to Tasks, Tests, and GitHub items. Empty states are handled by replacing the annotation icon with a subtle 'Create branch' / 'Add task' / 'Add test' inline affordance - so the same row promotes creation when no data exists. The pattern is consistent across User Story, Bug, Feature and Epic cards; only the available annotations differ (Tasks only appears when child tasks exist). Status is encoded in icon + colour together (never colour alone), text labels carry the canonical state name, and the dot-only pattern is reserved for pipeline-style strips. The aesthetic is utilitarian and dense, prioritising completeness of the link graph over visual minimalism - a useful contrast point for a Sand/Rams-restrained prototype that might pick a single composite badge over Azure DevOps's full multi-control panel.
